source_text: ὑπὲρ τῶν ἡμετέρων πλημμελημάτων παρεδόθη, διὰ ἡμᾶς τεθνάναι λέγεται. Ταύτῃ τοι καὶ ἡμεῖς οἱ σφάζοντες. Οἱ γὰρ δι' οὓς ἀπέθανεν ἀναγκαίως, μονονουχὶ τοῦ πάθους εἶεν ἂν ἐργάται σαφῶς, εἰ καὶ δρῷτό τι δι' ἑτέρων. Ὅτι δὲ σώζει τοὺς κεχρισμένους ὁ τοῦ αἵματος ῥαντισμὸς, παρέδειξεν εὐθὺς, χρῆναι τῷ αἵματι καταχρίειν εἰπὼν τῶν δωματίων τὰς εἰσβολὰς, σταθμῶν δὴ λέγω καὶ θυρῶν φλιάς. Ἀποφράττει γὰρ ὥσπερ καὶ ἀνέμβατον ἐργάζεται τῷ θανάτῳ τὴν εἰσβολὴν τὸ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον. Ἄραρεν οὖν, ὅτι τῷ τιμίῳ κατακεχρισμένοι καὶ ἡμεῖς αἵματι, θανάτου κρείττους ἐσόμεθα, καὶ φθορᾶς ἀλογήσομεν, δι' οὐδενὸς ποιούμενοι λόγου τὸν ὀλοθρευτήν. Ἐκρύεται γὰρ ἡμᾶς τὸ αἷμα τῆς ζωῆς, τουτέστι, Χριστοῦ. Χρῆναι δέ φησιν, ἐν νυκτὶ μιᾷ τὰ τοῦ ἀμνοῦ δαπανᾶσθαι κρέα· εἷς γὰρ ἀληθῶς, ὁ τοῦ σωτηρίου πάθους καιρὸς, καὶ ἅπαξ ἀποθανὼν, οὐκέτι ἀποθνήσκει, κατὰ τὸ γεγραμμένον, θάνατος αὐτοῦ οὐκέτι κυριεύσει· ὃ γὰρ ἀπέθανε, τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ ἀπέθανεν ἐφάπαξ· ὃ δὲ ζῇ, ζῇ τῷ Θεῷ. Ὀπτὰ δὲ τὰ κρέα, καὶ ἐπ' ἄρτοις ἀζύμοις ἐσθίεται καὶ πικρίσι, τοῦ μὲν ὀπτοῦ, τὴν οἱονεί πως διὰ παθημάτων τοῦ Ἐμμανουὴλ ὑπεμφαίνοντος τελείωσιν. «Ἔδει γὰρ, ἔδει, φησὶ, τὸν ἀρχηγὸν τῆς σωτηρίας ἡμῶν, διὰ παθημάτων τελειῶσαι.» Τοῦ γε μὴν ἐπ' ἀζύμων ἐσθίεσθαι καὶ πικρίδων, αἰνιγματωδῶς ὑπογράφοντος, ὅτι δεήσει καὶ ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς, οἷς ἂν παρακέοιτο πρὸς μέθεξιν ὁ Χριστὸς, ζύμης ἀπηλλάχθαι τῆς νοητῆς, τουτέστι, κακίας καὶ δόλου, ἀγαπᾷν δὲ ὅτι μάλιστα καὶ τὸ τληπαθεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν ἀγάπης, καὶ πικρῶν ἀνέχεσθαι πόνων, κατόπιν ἰόντας τοῦ δι' ἡμᾶς εἰς θάνατον εἰσελθόντος. Εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ παραθήγων ἡμᾶς, «Οὐκ ἔστι, φησὶ, μαθητὴς ὑπὲρ τὸν διδάσκαλον, οὐδὲ δοῦλος ὑπὲρ τὸν κύριον αὐτοῦ.» «Εἰ ἐμὲ ἐδίωξαν, καὶ ὑμᾶς διώξουσιν· εἰ τὸν οἰκοδεσπότην Βεελζεβοὺλ ἐπεκάλεσαν, πολλῷ μᾶλλον τοὺς οἰκειακοὺς αὐτοῦ. Ἀποφάσκει δὴ οὖν ὁ νόμος, τὸ δεῖν ἐσθίειν ὠμὸν, καὶ μέν τοι ἑψημένον ὕδατι, καί τοι μηδενὸς ἂν, οἶμαι, φαγόντος ὠμὸν, κἂν εἰ μὴ ἔφη τυχὸν ὁ νόμος. Ὑποφαίνει τοίνυν αἰνιγματωδῶς, ὅτι τὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ μυστήριον, οὔτε τὸ ἀπρόσβλητον ἔχει διὰ ψευσμάτων ὑπερβολὴν οὔτε μὴν τὸ ὑδαρὲς καὶ ἐκλελυμένον. Ἑλλήνων μὲν γὰρ οἱ λογάδες ποιηταί τε καὶ συγγραφεῖς, καὶ ὅσον ἧκεν εἰς λόγους σοφοὶ, τὰ τῶν παρὰ σφίσι θεῶν ἀναγράφοντες ὄργια, ψευδοεποῦσιν ἀγρίως, καὶ οἱονεί πως ὠμά τε καὶ ἀπαράδεκτα ταῖς ἀνθρώπων διανοίαις παραφέρουσι διηγήματα, καὶ πολὺ τὸ ὑδαρὲς, ἔν γε δὴ σφίσιν αὐτοῖς, κατηῤῥωστηκότα. Μοιχεῖαί τε γὰρ καὶ γυναίων ἔρωτες, καὶ μειρακίων διαφθοραὶ, καὶ αἰδοίων ἀποκοπαὶ, καὶ παρθένων εἰς δένδρα μεταφυτεύσεις, καὶ ἕτερα ἄττα πρὸς τούτοις πάναισχρά τε καὶ ἀκαλλῆ, μυθάρια τὰ παρ' αὐτοῖς νοούμενα, ἀλήθεια δέ ἐστι, πάντα τὰ ἐν Χριστῷ, εὐπαράδεκτά τε καὶ ἐδώδιμα νῷ, καὶ τὸ χαῦνον, ἢ ὑδαρὲς οὐκ ἔχοντα. Συνάγει γὰρ μᾶλλον εἰς εὐκοσμίαν τοὺς ἐθέλοντας νοεῖν, ἤπερ ἀνίησιν εἰς τρυφὰς καὶ φιλοσαρκίαν, καθάπερ ἀμέλει καὶ τὰ Ἑλ
pass_a_gloss: (For since) he was handed over for our trespasses, he is said to have died through (because of) us. For this reason we too (are) the ones slaughtering. For those through whom he died necessarily would be clearly all but workers of the suffering, even if something was done through others. And that the sprinkling of the blood saves those anointed, he showed at once, saying that one must anoint with the blood the entrances of the rooms, I mean of doorposts and lintels of doors. For the mystery of Christ blocks up and as it were makes the entrance unenterable for death. It is fixed then that we too, anointed with the precious blood, will be stronger than death, and will disregard corruption, making the destroyer of no account. For the blood of life rescues us, that is, of Christ. And he says the meats of the lamb must be spent in one night; for truly one is the season of the saving suffering, and having died once he dies no longer, according to what is written: death will no longer lord over him; for what he died, he died to sin once for all; and what he lives, he lives to God. And the meats (are) roasted, and are eaten upon unleavened loaves and bitter herbs, the roasting hinting at the as-it-were perfecting through sufferings of Emmanuel: 'For it was needful, needful,' he says, 'to perfect the leader of our salvation through sufferings.' And the being eaten upon unleavened (bread) and bitter herbs sketching in a riddle that it will be necessary for us ourselves too, before whom Christ might be laid out for partaking, to have been freed from the intelligible leaven, that is, malice and deceit, and to love most of all also the suffering-patiently for the love toward him, and to bear bitter toils, going behind the one who entered into death for us. For sharpening us toward this he says: 'A disciple is not above the teacher, nor a slave above his lord.' 'If they persecuted me they will persecute you too; if they called the master of the house Beelzebul, much more those of his household.' The law then forbids that one must eat raw, and also boiled in water, although nobody, I think, would eat raw, even if the law perhaps did not say. It hints then in a riddle that the mystery of Christ has neither the unapproachable through excess of lies nor the watery and loosened. For the select poets and writers of the Greeks, and as many as are wise as far as words go, writing up the rites of the gods among them, lie savagely, and bring to the minds of men tales as it were raw and unacceptable, and much watery (stuff) grown sickly among them. For adulteries and loves of women, and corruptions of youths, and cuttings off of genitals, and transplantings of maidens into trees, and some other things besides these all-shameful and ugly, (are) the little myths understood among them; but truth is all the things in Christ, easily received and edible for the mind, and not having the slack or watery. For it gathers rather into good order those wishing to understand than lets loose into luxuries and flesh-love, as indeed the (cold and old-womanish tales) of the Greeks (continues).
pass_b_english: Cyril: …he was handed over for our trespasses, he is said to have died because of us. That is why we too are the ones who slaughter it. For those on whose account he necessarily died would plainly be, all but, the doers of the suffering, even if something was done by the hands of others. That the sprinkling of the blood saves those who have been anointed with it, he showed at once by saying that the entrances of the rooms must be smeared with the blood, I mean the doorposts and the lintels of the doors. For the mystery of Christ blocks the entrance against death and makes it, as it were, impassable to it. It stands firm, then, that we too, anointed with the precious blood, will be stronger than death and will think nothing of corruption, making no account of the destroyer. For the blood of life, that is, of Christ, rescues us.

He says that the flesh of the lamb must be consumed in a single night. For truly the time of the saving suffering is one; and ‘having died once, he dies no more,’ as it is written; ‘death will no longer have dominion over him. For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God’ (Romans 6:9–10). The flesh is roasted, and it is eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The roasting hints at the perfecting, so to speak, of Emmanuel through sufferings: ‘For it was fitting, truly fitting,’ it says, ‘to make the author of our salvation perfect through sufferings’ (Hebrews 2:10). Its being eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs sketches in a riddle that we ourselves, before whom Christ is set to share, must be rid of the leaven of the mind, that is, of malice and deceit, and must love above all to endure suffering for love of him and to bear bitter labors, following after the one who for our sake went into death. To spur us on to this he says: ‘A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master’ (Matthew 10:24). ‘If they persecuted me, they will persecute you too’ (John 15:20). ‘If they called the master of the house Beelzebul, how much more those of his household’ (Matthew 10:25).

Then the law forbids eating it raw, and boiled in water as well, although no one, I think, would have eaten it raw even if the law had not happened to say so. So it suggests in a riddle that the mystery of Christ has neither the repulsiveness that comes from an excess of falsehoods nor anything watery and slack. For the choice poets and prose writers of the Greeks, and all who were wise as far as words go, when they record the rites of their gods, tell outrageous lies and serve up to human minds tales that are, so to speak, raw and unacceptable; and much that is watery and sickly has a hold among them. Adulteries and passions for women, the corruption of boys, the cutting off of private parts, maidens changed into trees, and other things besides, utterly shameful and ugly: these are the little myths they believe. But all that is in Christ is truth, easily received and good food for the mind, with nothing slack or watery in it. For it draws those who are willing to understand toward good order, rather than letting them loose into luxury and love of the flesh, as the Greeks'…

choices.english: would plainly be, all but, the doers of the suffering
choices.why: Keeps Cyril's hedge μονονουχί and the potential mood.

choices.english: For it was fitting, truly fitting
choices.why: Cyril's doubled ἔδει in his form of Hebrews 2:10 (ἔπρεπεν in the epistle).
ἀγρίως intensifies; 'savagely' read oddly in English.
